newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan rebels threaten Kabul after key town falls.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels threaten Kabul after key town falls.

text.p: The Afghan Taleban militia thrust towards Kabul and a government airbase on Wednesday after capturing the strategic town of Sarobi overnight.

Taleban forces pushed up the main Jalalabad-Kabul highway as far as Mahipur, only 25 km (16 miles) from the city, Taleban sources said. They said government troops had blown up a bridge at Mahipur, but Taleban fighters had crossed the area on foot.
Prime Minister Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's Hezb-i-Islami faction, which had controlled Sarobi, confirmed the Taleban had seized the town, 70 km (44 miles) east of the Afghan capital.
"Sarobi has fallen and Hezb-i-Islami fighters blew up an ammunition dump and some vehicles as they retreated," said a Hezb-i-Islami source in the Pakistani city of Peshawar.
The capture of Sarobi was the latest in a series of spectacular Taleban gains in eastern Afghanistan this month and a big setback to President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government.
It was another blow to Hekmatyar, who has now lost virtually all the territory previously controlled by Hezb-i-Islami.
The government, hemmed in by the latest Taleban advances, turned to opposition militia commander General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who controls Kabul's last supply route to the north.
An Islamabad-based official of Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli faction said Interior Minister Yunus Qanuni was holding talks with Dostum in Uzbekistan's capital Tashkent on Wednesday.
He said Dostum had left for Tashkent four days ago for medical treatment. Qanuni had joined him there on Tuesday.
Mohammad said he had no information about the talks, but added that Dostum would not support any Taleban attack on Kabul.

Dostum is an opponent of Rabbani, but is despised by the Taleban for his communist background. Last month he agreed to reopen the strategic Salang highway linking Kabul with the north as part of a truce with government forces.
U.N. sources in Kabul said the city was calm despite the Taleban advances and the streets were as busy as usual.
The Taleban seized Sarobi about midnight (1900 GMT Tuesday) in a two-pronged assault after resistance died away, Taleban sources in the Pakistani city of Peshawar said.
"Sarobi has been taken over completely," one source said. "Now, inshallah (God willing), we will reach Kabul."
The sources said the militia had taken the nearby Naghlu Dam and hydroelectric plant that began supplying power to parts of Kabul only 10 days ago after a break of two and a half years.
They said the Islamic rebels were advancing northwards from Naghlu up the Tagab Valley leading to the main government airbase at Bagram, 50 km (31 miles) north of Kabul.
The Taleban were also attacking frontlines near the village of Band-i-Ghazi southeast of Kabul and one source said they planned to launch other assaults from the south and west.

Two government jets dropped at least three bombs on the Taleban-held airport at Jalalabad on Wednesday, but failed to damage airport buildings, Taleban sources said. A government plane dropped cluster bombs near the airport on Tuesday.

The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted Taleban sources as saying the government had lost hundreds of dead in and around Sarobi, while 105 had been captured. At least 14 Taleban fighters had been killed and 25 wounded.
Kabul radio, monitored in Islamabad, said government forces had killed 100 rebels and destroyed many military vehicles in Tuesday's battle for Sarobi, but did not report Taleban gains.
On Tuesday, the government-run radio said rockets fired by the Taleban killed three civilians and wounded nine in Kabul.
The Islamic rebels have tightened their grip on eastern provinces this month as part of a drive to seize Kabul, oust Rabbani and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan.
The Afghan government has often accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban. Islamabad denies the charge.
